readerTitle: The idea nobody wanted that earned $100 million a year
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Microsoft Bing 광고 제목 실험) + 실제 연구 (Microsoft 실험 성공률) + 가상 적용 (카페, 레스토랑)
insight: 성장 아이디어는 모두 추측이다. 누가 더 좋은 아이디어를 내느냐보다 얼마나 싸고 공정하게 많이 시험하느냐가 성장을 만든다.
misconception: 경험 많은 사람은 어떤 아이디어가 먹힐지 안다. 바꾼 뒤 매출이 올랐으면 그 변화 덕분이다.

sources.text: Kohavi, R. & Thomke, S. (2017). The Surprising Power of Online Experiments. Harvard Business Review, Sept–Oct 2017.
Kohavi, R., Tang, D. & Xu, Y. (2020). Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments. Cambridge University Press.

factChecks.note: Bing 광고 제목 사례(2012년경): 아이디어가 6개월 넘게 우선순위 목록에 묻혀 있었고, 엔지니어가 며칠 만에 구현해 테스트, 매출 12% 증가, 미국에서만 연간 1억 달러 이상. Kohavi & Thomke(2017) 원문에서 수치와 기간을 게시 전 다시 확인하세요.
'Microsoft에서 시험한 아이디어 중 목표 지표를 개선한 것은 약 3분의 1'이라는 내용은 Kohavi & Thomke(2017)와 Kohavi 외(2020)에 나옵니다. 카드에는 "about a third"로만 적었습니다. 원문 표현을 확인하세요.
카페와 레스토랑 사례에는 수치를 넣지 않았습니다. 모든 장면은 가상입니다.

cards.title: The idea nobody wanted that earned $100 million a year
body: Around 2012, someone at Microsoft suggested a small change to how ads looked on Bing, its search engine. Make the ad headlines a bit longer.
Managers ranked it low. It sat on a to-do list for more than six months. Then an engineer tried it in a few days.

image.label: A sticky note buried at the bottom of a long to-do list
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 길게 늘어진 할 일 목록 맨 아래에 먼지 쌓인 작은 포스트잇 하나. 그 포스트잇에서만 은은한 빛이 남. 실제 회사 로고나 검색엔진 화면은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Fifty ideas, time for five.
body: You lead growth at an online business. Your team has a list of 50 ideas to win more customers. You only have time to fully build five this quarter.
How do you choose?

options.text: Build the five your most experienced people rank highest
options.feedback: Experience narrows the list fast. But you'll never learn whether the low-ranked ideas were better, and rankings are often wrong.

options.text: Run quick, cheap tests on many ideas, then build what wins
options.feedback: You spend a little on each idea and let customer behavior pick the winners. The cost is setting up tests you can trust.

options.text: Survey customers and build the ideas they like most
options.feedback: It feels customer-led, but people are poor at predicting what they'll actually click, buy or come back for.

cards.title: Revenue jumped 12%.
body: The engineer showed the longer headlines to some users and the old ones to others, then compared.
The new version raised ad revenue by about **12%**. In the US alone, that was worth more than $100 million a year.
Nobody had predicted it. The people who knew the business best had put it near the bottom of the list.

cards.title: Growth experiments
body: A **growth experiment** tests one change on some customers while others get the usual version. You pick the measure of success *before* you start, then compare the two groups.
The comparison group is the key. It shows what would have happened without the change, so weather, season or luck don't fool you.

image.label: Customers split into two groups, one sees a change
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 손님 아이콘들이 입구에서 무작위로 두 줄로 나뉨. 왼쪽 'Usual version', 오른쪽 'One change'. 끝에 같은 저울 위에 두 결과가 올라감. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Most good-sounding ideas don't work.
body: Ronny Kohavi, who led experiments at Microsoft, reported that only about **a third** of tested ideas improved the result they were meant to improve. The rest did nothing or made things worse.
So the goal isn't to have only good ideas. Nobody does. The goal is to test many ideas cheaply and keep the few that win.

cards.title: A café can run experiments too.
body: A café adds a breakfast combo in March and sales rise. Did the combo work? Maybe. Or spring arrived and more people walked by.
A fairer test: offer the combo on randomly chosen days for four weeks. Compare those days with the others on one measure picked in advance, like average spend per customer.
No software needed. Just a split, a measure and patience.

image.label: Café calendar with some days marked for a test
image.brief: 카페 카운터 벽의 월간 달력. 무작위로 고른 날짜에만 작은 토스트 스티커가 붙어 있고, 옆에 손글씨 메모 'Avg spend per customer'. 따뜻한 색감, 실제 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Experiments need enough customers and the right measure.
body: With few customers, small differences are just noise. A small business should test bold changes and run tests longer.
Pick the measure carefully. A pushy upsell can lift today's spend and quietly drive regulars away. Check what happens weeks later, not just on the day.
And decide when the test ends before you start. Stopping the moment numbers look good is how lucky results get mistaken for wins.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant.
body: You run a 30-table restaurant. Your chef thinks a small card on each table showing tonight's dessert will sell more desserts.
How do you find out?

options.text: Put cards on every table this month and compare with last month
options.feedback: Easy to run, but holidays, weather and menu changes all differ between months. You can't tell what caused any change.

options.text: Put cards on half the tables, swap halves each night, and count desserts per table for a month
options.feedback: Both groups share the same nights and kitchen, so the card is the main difference. It takes a month of careful counting.

options.text: Ask your regulars whether a card would tempt them
options.feedback: Cheap and you may hear useful ideas. But what diners say about dessert and what they order are often different.

cards.title: Treat every growth idea as a guess worth testing.
body: Change one thing for some customers, keep a comparison group, and decide in advance what success looks like.
**Try it today:** pick one idea you've been debating. Write down the change, who gets it, who doesn't, and the one number that will decide.
